title: not fit to be called an Apostle?
opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
prayer: Jesus, give me a new love. Give me Your love. And teach me to go in peace. Amen.
body:
For several days now, I have been struggling. My mind keeps wandering backward—to mistakes I have made, things I have said, the person I once was, and things that simply cannot be undone.

I have always struggled somewhat with people. Trust has never come easily to me. Somewhere along the way, perhaps much earlier than I realized, I learned to protect myself by keeping a certain distance. Rejection has a way of doing that. Eventually the protection that keeps us from being hurt can also make it difficult to love freely.

Yesterday, when I read Paul's words about love in 1 Corinthians 12:31–13:13, I found myself wondering: What if I haven't loved well enough?

That question has stayed with me.

I don't mean that I don't want to love. Quite the opposite. I want the kind of love Paul describes—patient, kind, not jealous, not quick-tempered, not keeping an account of injuries. But when I honestly examine my own heart, I recognize how difficult some of those things have been for me.

So lately I have been asking Jesus for something very simple:  Give me a new love. Give me Your love, because mine is not enough.

Then today's readings seemed to answer me.

Paul tells us that he considers himself the least of the Apostles, "not fit to be called an Apostle," because he had persecuted the Church of God. Paul couldn't change what he had done. He couldn't return to his former life and erase it.

Neither can we.

But then Paul says something extraordinary:

"But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace to me has not been ineffective."

I needed those words.

My past may explain something about me, but it does not have to be the final definition of me. God's grace can still accomplish something with the person standing here today.

Then the Gospel takes us into the home of Simon the Pharisee, where a woman known as a sinner approaches Jesus. She stands behind Him weeping. Her tears fall upon His feet. She wipes them with her hair, kisses His feet and anoints them.

Simon watches all of this and judges her.

Jesus knows exactly what Simon is thinking.

Then comes a sentence that almost stops me every time I read it:

"Simon, I have something to say to you."

Imagine sitting beside Jesus and hearing Him say your name followed by those words.

Jesus tells Simon about two people who owed debts, one much greater than the other. Neither could repay what was owed, so the creditor forgave both debts. Jesus asks which person would love the creditor more.

Simon answers, "The one, I suppose, whose larger debt was forgiven."

Jesus tells him that he has judged rightly.

Then Jesus turns toward the woman and says:

"Her many sins have been forgiven; hence, she has shown great love. But the one to whom little is forgiven, loves little."

At first, those words frightened me.

I wondered whether Jesus was saying that if I have not loved enough, perhaps I have not been forgiven.

But perhaps I had it backward.

The woman isn't forgiven because she managed to produce enough love. Her love pours out because she has encountered mercy.

She knows she needs Jesus.

Simon is looking across the room at someone else's sins. The woman is at the feet of Christ with her own.

And suddenly I understood something about love.

Maybe learning to love doesn't begin by forcing ourselves to feel differently about everyone. Maybe it begins by understanding how much mercy we ourselves have received.

Love can look very ordinary.

It can mean refusing to return an injury. It can mean being slower to judge. It can mean forgiving someone even when the memory still hurts. It can mean having mercy on someone whose story we don't understand. Sometimes it may simply mean praying, "Jesus, I cannot love this person the way You ask me to. Please love them through me."

And perhaps we need to offer some of that mercy to ourselves as well.

There are things in my past that I regret. Some can be repaired; others cannot. I can confess them. I can ask forgiveness. I can make amends where possible. But I cannot travel backward and become someone else.

Neither could Paul.

Yet Paul did not spend the rest of his life introducing himself only as the man who persecuted Christians.

He said:

"By the grace of God I am what I am."

There is a difference between remembering our sins so that they lead us toward repentance and endlessly replaying them until they lead us toward despair.

One brings us to the feet of Jesus.

The other keeps us staring at ourselves.

So perhaps when those old thoughts return, the prayer doesn't need to be complicated:

Jesus, I give You what I was.
I give You what I did.
I give You the people who hurt me and the people I have hurt.
Teach me to forgive.
Teach me to receive forgiveness.
And give me enough of Your love that I can give some of it away today.

I still struggle with this. I still have moments of judgment, mistrust, resentment and fear. I don't understand where every feeling comes from, and I don't know that I need to understand everything before bringing it to Christ.

I only need to keep coming.

Because at the end of the Gospel, Jesus does not tell the woman to spend the rest of her life terrified about whether she has been forgiven enough.

He tells her:

"Your faith has saved you; go in peace."

Maybe those words are meant for more of us than we realize.

We cannot undo yesterday. But by the grace of God, yesterday does not have to determine what we do with today.

And so today I will ask again:
